value.overview: The White-chinned Swift (Cypseloides cryptus) is a small, fast-flying swift of tropical America. It spends most of its life in the air, catching insects over forests, hills, and open areas. The species is widely distributed but locally uncommon and patchy, and much of its biology remains poorly documented. Costa Rica is especially important because it is one of the few countries where the species has been confirmed to breed.
value.classification: The White-chinned Swift belongs to the swift family Apodidae, in the genus Cypseloides. It is not closely related to swallows, although its streamlined shape and aerial habits can cause confusion.
value.identification: This swift is about 15 cm long, with a dark brown to blackish head, back, wings, and tail. The underparts are somewhat paler, and the white chin is the most useful distinguishing feature, although it can be difficult to see on a fast-flying bird. A short pale streak above the eye may also be visible. The sexes look alike. Identification is often based on a combination of structure, flight style, plumage, habitat, and calls rather than on a single field mark.
value.rangeHabitat: The White-chinned Swift occurs patchily from Mexico through Central America and into northern and western South America, reaching areas as far south as Peru and east to Suriname. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon to rare resident breeder, recorded mainly in mountainous regions and associated with humid forest. It generally uses open airspace above forest and valleys for feeding, while nesting sites are believed to include sheltered rock faces, caves, or areas associated with waterfalls and cliffs. Confirmed breeding records from Costa Rica make the country significant for the species.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the White-chinned Swift is generally treated as a resident breeder and possibly a permanent resident. Reliable evidence for regular long-distance migration is limited, although local or seasonal movements may occur and the species can be difficult to detect.
value.breeding: The species has been confirmed to breed in Costa Rica and at least one locality in northern Brazil, but detailed information on its nesting biology is limited. Like other Cypseloides swifts, it is expected to place its nest on a sheltered vertical surface, such as a cliff, cave wall, or site near falling water. Nesting birds may be particularly difficult to observe because they approach colonies rapidly and spend little time perched. A Costa Rican bird in breeding condition has been recorded in June.
value.dietFeeding: The White-chinned Swift feeds on flying insects and other small airborne arthropods. It forages almost entirely in flight, often traveling rapidly over humid forest, mountain slopes, valleys, and clearings. It may join mixed flocks of swifts and swallows where flying insects are concentrated. Its long, pointed wings and powerful flight allow it to cover large areas while feeding, but its aerial habits make direct study difficult.
value.behavior: This is a highly aerial species that usually remains in continuous flight and rarely perches in the open. It is fast and agile, with swift, direct movements and frequent changes in height and direction while foraging. Individuals may occur singly or in small groups, sometimes among other swifts. They are more likely to be detected by their flight silhouette or calls than by prolonged views, and nesting birds may gather near cliffs or waterfalls.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. The species is widespread but patchily distributed, and available information is limited, especially for population size and breeding colonies.
